segments.speaker: John
segments.text: In our graduate seminar on continual learning and language-model agents, today's lecture is on Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners? The Survey of Self-Evolving Agents and Harness Continual Learning reflect a growing interest in adapting agents without changing model weights. This paper, from a team that includes Google DeepMind researchers, tests whether those adaptations actually accumulate safely over time. The field is moving from asking whether agents can improve to asking whether they can improve without harming other tasks. Yes, Noah?

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Hi Professor, if the model weights stay fixed, what exactly is learning?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The agent's harness is learning: the surrounding instructions, memory, skill files, and code that coordinate its actions. Think of a fixed instrument with a changing operator's manual. The authors compare two broad strategies: self-modification, which changes shared instructions or infrastructure, and experience augmentation, which stores past examples for later retrieval. Their central question is whether feedback from one task produces transferable gains or creates interference as the agent encounters new tasks.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: To test that, the researchers build 4 task streams from the bird, B-F-C-L, and ScienceWorld benchmarks. Each stream has consecutive groups of 50 training tasks, but the agent is not told when groups change or given their labels. The shifts vary: database topics can change, workflows can demand different behavior, domains and tools can change, or several kinds of change can be combined. One shared harness must handle the whole stream.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Quick question: how do they distinguish learning a new task from forgetting an old one?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: They measure plasticity as the performance gain on a task group at the end of its training block. Stability captures losses elsewhere: both interference on groups not yet trained and forgetting on groups already encountered. They also report final and average accuracy changes relative to the initial harness. This matters because a strong final score can hide uneven learning. An agent might master its current task while quietly becoming less reliable on another.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: All methods use the same fixed Gemini 3.6 Flash model in a reasoning-and-action loop, so the comparison isolates changes to the harness. ReasoningBank stores experience-based memories and retrieves the single most similar one for each query. G-E-P-A uses feedback to rewrite a shared strategy section in the system prompt. Meta-Harness gives a coding agent a broader workspace to edit, including prompts, memory, skills, and controller code, with validation used to accept or reject edits.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Can a shared prompt really make performance worse on a task the agent has not learned yet?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Yes. In the compound stream, experience from database tasks encouraged exploratory tool use. Before training on B-F-C-L Miss, that guidance lowered its accuracy by 6.8 percentage points with G-E-P-A and 4.8 points with Meta-Harness. But B-F-C-L Miss requires asking for clarification when API arguments are missing. A generally useful instruction to investigate can become the wrong policy in a different workflow, like giving a careful lab protocol to someone who first needs to ask what materials are available.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Memory retrieval avoids rewriting one shared prompt, but it does not guarantee that a recalled experience is appropriate. ReasoningBank always inserts its closest match, even when the task group has not yet supplied relevant examples. The workflow groups B-F-C-L Miss and B-F-C-L Base have highly similar query embeddings despite requiring conflicting behavior. At the end of the streams, many episodes in each group retrieved memories from the other, showing that topical resemblance does not ensure procedural compatibility.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Hold on, the streams have fixed blocks. How far can we generalize these results to real deployments?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: That is an important limitation. Across the 12 method-and-scenario comparisons, stronger plasticity correlated with worse stability. G-E-P-A had the largest average plasticity gain, 6.2 percentage points, but also the greatest stability loss, minus 4.3 points. The experiments use one underlying model, 3 methods, benchmark-derived tasks, and block-structured streams. They reveal concrete risks under those conditions, not a universal ranking of every agent or a complete picture of open-ended deployment.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The paper shifts evaluation toward the full learning trajectory, not just a benchmark endpoint. That complements surveys mapping what parts of agents can evolve and work such as Harness Continual Learning, which treats prompts, memory, and skills as adaptation state. The contribution here is to show why editable state needs careful control: shared changes can spread too broadly, and retrieved experiences can collide. Future systems will need ways to identify context and check whether a lesson applies before using it.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: So the key challenge is deciding when stored knowledge applies, not merely how to store it?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Exactly. Continual adaptation is not simply accumulating instructions or memories; it requires preserving boundaries between tasks with different needs. This study gives researchers practical tests for that problem: track learning and degradation across a stream, inspect which memories are retrieved, and check how shared edits affect untrained tasks. For deployed agents, reliable evolution may depend as much on selective application as on acquiring new experience. Thanks for listening.
